candidate_concepts.label: Bag of Words (BoW) Definition
candidate_concepts.description: Bag of Words is a method to extract features from text documents by creating a vocabulary of all unique words and representing documents as vectors of word counts, ignoring word order.
coverage_criteria: Student can state that BoW is a text representation technique that uses word frequency vectors.
Student can explain that BoW disregards grammar and word order.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article defines BoW explicitly: 'Bag of Words (BOW) is a method to extract features from text documents... It creates a vocabulary of all the unique words...'
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a core concept that can be assessed with a single definitional question and is foundational for later candidates.

candidate_concepts.label: BoW Pipeline Steps
candidate_concepts.description: The typical BoW process involves cleaning text, tokenizing (splitting into words), building a vocabulary of unique terms, and generating numeric vectors of word counts for each document.
coverage_criteria: Student can list the main steps: clean, tokenize, build vocabulary, generate vectors.
Student can describe that vocabulary is the set of all unique words from all documents.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article shows a workflow diagram and describes: 'On a high level, it involves the following steps... clean text, tokenize, build vocabulary, and generate vectors.'
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This breaks down the process into a verifiable sequence of steps, each of which can be checked individually.

candidate_concepts.label: Tokenization and Stopword Removal
candidate_concepts.description: Tokenization is the process of splitting text into tokens (words). Stopwords (e.g., 'a', 'the') are common words with little significance that are often removed to reduce noise and vocabulary size.
coverage_criteria: Student can define tokenization as breaking text into words/tokens.
Student can explain that stopwords are filtered out because they lack useful information for many NLP tasks.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article states: 'Tokenization is the act of breaking up a sequence of strings into pieces...' and defines stopwords: 'words which do not contain enough significance...'
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a well-defined subtask of text preprocessing that can be checked with a short exercise or definition.

candidate_concepts.label: BoW Vector Representation and Vocabulary Size
candidate_concepts.description: Each document is converted to a fixed-length vector equal to the vocabulary size. Each position corresponds to a word, and the value is the count of that word in the document.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that a document vector length equals the number of unique words in the vocabulary.
Student can compute a simple BoW vector from given word counts.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article illustrates with examples: 'The length of the vector will always be equal to vocabulary size.' and shows vectors for sentences.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific, checkable understanding of how BoW vectors are constructed; suitable for a numeric example question.

candidate_concepts.label: Sparse Vectors Problem
candidate_concepts.description: When the vocabulary is large, document vectors become mostly zeros (sparse). Sparse vectors require significant memory and computation, posing challenges for machine learning algorithms.
coverage_criteria: Student can define a sparse vector as one with many zero entries.
Student can explain why sparsity is problematic for ML modeling (memory, computational complexity).

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article warns: 'A big document where the generated vocabulary is huge may result in a vector with lots of 0 values. This is called a sparse vector.' and notes the resource demands.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single, well-defined disadvantage that can be checked with a short explanation.

source_anchors.locator: This is called a sparse vector. Sparse vectors require more memory and computational resources...

candidate_concepts.label: Implementing BoW in Python
candidate_concepts.description: The BoW algorithm can be implemented in Python by writing functions to clean and tokenize text, build a vocabulary from all sentences, and generate count vectors using a fixed vocabulary.
coverage_criteria: Student can outline the key Python functions: word extraction with regex and stopword removal, vocabulary collection, and vector generation using NumPy.
Student can identify that vector generation iterates over each sentence and increments counts for known vocabulary words.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article provides a complete Python implementation with functions: word_extraction, tokenize, and generate_bow.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical coding concept that can be assessed by asking students to explain the code or complete similar functions.

candidate_concepts.label: Using NLTK for Stopwords
candidate_concepts.description: Instead of manually listing stopwords, Python's NLTK library provides predefined language-specific stopword lists, such as nltk.corpus.stopwords.words('english').
coverage_criteria: Student can recall that NLTK offers a built-in stopwords corpus.
Student can write a snippet to import stopwords from NLTK.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article mentions: 'For more robust implementation of stopwords, you can use python nltk library.' and gives an example.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a small, checkable tool-specific fact that supports the BoW implementation.

candidate_concepts.label: CountVectorizer from scikit-learn
candidate_concepts.description: Scikit-learn's CountVectorizer provides a ready-to-use BoW implementation, converting a collection of text documents to a matrix of token counts.

candidate_concepts.label: Limitations of BoW
candidate_concepts.description: BoW ignores semantic meaning and word order, making it unable to capture context or phrases. It also produces large sparse vectors for large vocabularies.
coverage_criteria: Student can state that BoW loses semantic meaning and context.
Student can explain that large vocabularies lead to high-dimensional sparse vectors.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article explicitly lists limitations: 'Semantic meaning: ... It completely ignores the context...' and 'Vector size: For a large document, the vector size can be huge...'
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a concise, assessable set of disadvantages that can be checked with a single question.

candidate_concepts.label: N-gram Extension to BoW
candidate_concepts.description: To capture some word order, BoW can be extended to n-grams (e.g., bigrams), where tokens are pairs of consecutive words, providing a richer representation.
coverage_criteria: Student can define an n-gram as a contiguous sequence of n words.
Student can explain that bigrams (2-grams) can improve representation by considering word pairs.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article mentions: 'For example, instead of splitting our sentence in a single word (1-gram), you can split in the pair of two words (bi-gram or 2-gram).'
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a small, distinct extension that can be checked with a definition and simple example.
